records.name: Gedvilė
records.facts_used: Gedvilė is a Lithuanian two-stem feminine name paired with masculine Gedvilas, which Salys lists among names with the element vil-. In his stem list he compares ged- with (pasi)gesti, gedėti and gedauti, verbs of longing or missing, and vil- with viltis “hope”. These comparisons explain the separate elements, not a single literal sentence. Pakerys reports that the 1934 “Didysis kalendorius” included about fifty two-stem feminine names, naming Gedvilė among its examples. This dates a printed calendar record; it does not identify the first girl to receive the name.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Pakerys 2011, PDF 1 / printed 90, visually checked: Gedvilė among examples in the 1934 “Didysis kalendorius”; PDF 2 / printed 91 cites the 1948 spelling dictionary Gedvilas, -ė. Salys stem list PDF 287 / printed 272: Ged-, Ges- : (pasi)gesti : gedėti : gedauti; PDF 298 / printed 283: Vil- : viltis, with Lithuanian Gedvilas.

records.name: Marijus
records.facts_used: The Senn–Salys Lithuanian–German dictionary gives Marijus as the personal name corresponding to Marius and Mario, with Marius as its short form. Behind the Name lists Marijus as the Lithuanian variant of Marius, a Roman family name derived either from Mars or from Latin mas, maris “male”; the alternatives are kept open. The 1964 Lithuanian name calendar compiled by Yla and Salys, reprinted in Salys’s 1983 collected writings, lists Marijus (with short form Marys) on 19 January beside Kanutas and Pija. This is a dated calendar record; it does not mark the first Lithuanian bearer.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Senn–Salys dictionary in Salys 1983, PDF 250 / printed 235, visually checked: Marijus PN Marius, Mario; Marius KF of Marijus. 1964 calendar PDF 301 / printed 286, visually checked: 19 January Kanutas (Kanas), Marijus (Marys), Pija. Behind the Name Marius lists Marijus (Lithuanian); Mars / mas, maris alternatives kept.

records.name: Kleopatra
records.facts_used: The Senn–Salys dictionary records Kleopatra as a personal name corresponding to German Kleopatra. Behind the Name explains the Greek name Kleopatra as “glory of the father”, from kleos “glory” and pater “father”. It was borne by queens of Ptolemaic Egypt, but those ancient bearers do not date the Lithuanian spelling. The 1964 Lithuanian name calendar reprinted by Salys in 1983 lists Kleopatra, with short forms Kleopa and Patra, on 19 October. That historical date differs from the project calendar’s 19 January and is kept as a separate dated record, not a correction.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Senn–Salys PDF 241 / printed 226, visually checked: Kleopatrà PN Kleopatra. 1964 calendar PDF 315 / printed 300 (October section), visually checked: 19 Kleopatra (Kleopa, Patra). Behind the Name Cleopatra: kleos + pater. Historical 19 October date kept distinct from project 19 January.

records.name: Hendrik
records.facts_used: Edgar Rajandi refers Hendrik to Heinrich and lists Endrik ~ Hendrik among the usual Estonian forms of that name. He derives Heinrich from East Frankish Haimrich, “master in his own home”, while noting that the original form and meaning are not entirely clear; a derivation from Hagenrich, “ruler of the court”, is also cited. Julius Mägiste’s 1929 collection of Estonian personal names already lists Hendrik among its men’s names, citing Wiedemann’s dictionary. Rajandi’s 1966 book adds that the Heinrich family spread more widely in Estonia from the fifteenth century. Neither date marks the first Hendrik.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Rajandi PDF 75 / printed 77 (Hendo, Hendrik → Heinrich) and PDF 71–72 / printed 73–74 (Heinrich article: Haimrich, Hagenrich alternative, Endrik ~ Hendrik, spread from the 15th century), visually checked. Mägiste 1929 PDF 27 / printed 25, visually checked: Hendrik -u (Wd., Rnm.).

records.name: Henri
records.facts_used: Rajandi lists Henri ~ Henry as forms that refer back to Heinrich, and mentions Henriette as the sister name of French Henri. Rajandi derives Heinrich from East Frankish Haimrich, “master in his own home”, while noting that the original form and meaning are not entirely clear. The family link does not make every Henri a borrowing from one particular language. Statistics Estonia counted 2,055 men named Henri on 1 January 2026. The oldest were in the 75–79 age group, while the name was most frequent relative to population among boys aged 5–9, documenting both earlier use and a recent rise.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.

records.name: Heino
records.facts_used: Rajandi gives Heino two documented contexts: it stands beside Eino, which he links with the old German Einewald, but he states that Heino is much older than Eino and mostly derives from Heinrich. Rajandi derives Heinrich from East Frankish Haimrich, “master in his own home”, while noting that the original form and meaning are not entirely clear. Rajandi’s 1966 book names Enn, Heino and Harri as the favourite Heinrich variants a generation earlier, and lists Heino among the forms still preferred, with Harri, Heiki and Indrek, at a combined 20–25 per thousand. Mägiste’s 1929 list already records Hein ~ Heino.

records.name: Henn
records.facts_used: Rajandi groups Henn ~ Henno ~ Hennu with Heinrich and with the related short forms Enn, Enni and Enno. He presents Heinrich as having produced an exceptional number of Estonian variants. Rajandi derives Heinrich from East Frankish Haimrich, “master in his own home”, while noting that the original form and meaning are not entirely clear. Rajandi reports that names such as Enn, Henn, Henu, Eno, Henno and Henni occur often in Estonian documents of the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries. In his analysis of 10,000 names given in 1935–1955, Henn occurred 15 times, compared with 63 for Enn.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.

records.name: Enno

records.name: Eno
records.facts_used: Rajandi gives Eno ~ Enu two separate uses: as a woman’s name it belongs with Ene, and as a man’s name it equals Enn, a short form from the Heinrich family. Mägiste’s 1929 list likewise places Eno next to Enn for comparison. The masculine Heinrich link therefore does not cover every bearer. Rajandi names Eno among forms such as Enn, Henn, Henu, Henno and Henni found in Estonian documents of the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries. Statistics Estonia counted 70 men and fewer than five women named Eno on 1 January 2026, so both uses continue.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Rajandi PDF 54 / printed 56, visually checked: Eno ~ Enu, as women’s name → Ene, as men’s name = Enn; PDF 53 / printed 55: Eno among 14th–16th-century document forms. records.name: Heigo
